question: If you strip a complete ring of bark from around a tree's trunk but leave the wood underneath untouched, the tree will usually die within a year or two, even though it keeps drawing up water and leafing out at first. Why?
correct_answer: Bark carries sugars down; roots starve
alternative_answers: The phloem in the bark is cut, so food can't reach the roots
Sugars from the leaves can no longer travel down to the roots
The roots starve because nutrient flow in the bark is severed
Girdling cuts the tree's food-transport layer
The roots die from lack of food and then the tree can't take up water
headline_answer: Bark carries sugars down; roots starve
source_excerpt: Girdling results in the removal of the phloem, and death occurs from the inability of the leaves to transport sugars (primarily sucrose) to the roots.

extra.verification_notes: Girdling removes phloem, so sugars can't reach the roots and they starve, while the xylem keeps carrying water; this matches the claimed answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girdling).

explanation: A tree moves things in two separate systems. Water and minerals travel upward through the wood, the xylem, so an intact trunk still delivers water to the leaves. But the sugars the leaves produce travel downward through the phloem, a thin living layer in the inner bark. Removing a full ring of bark severs the phloem completely, so no sugar can reach the roots. The roots slowly starve, stop growing and eventually stop taking up water, and the tree dies. This is called girdling or ring-barking, and foresters and farmers have used it deliberately for centuries to kill unwanted trees.

question: Wine corks are punched from the thick outer bark of which kind of tree?
source_excerpt: It is the phellem layer of bark tissue which is harvested for commercial use primarily from Quercus suber (the cork oak)

extra.why_interesting: Most people never connect the stopper in a wine bottle to a living tree that is peeled, not felled, and goes on growing new bark for a century.
extra.verification_notes: Cork is harvested mainly from the bark of the cork oak (Quercus suber), and stoppers are its main use, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cork_(material).

explanation: The cork oak is stripped by hand about every nine years and simply regrows its bark, which is why Portugal's cork forests are centuries old and still productive.

question: The pain-relieving compound that chemists later turned into aspirin was first extracted from the bark of which tree?
source_excerpt: the bitter taste of willow bark resembled the taste of the bark of the cinchona tree

extra.why_interesting: A modern pharmacy staple traces straight back to a riverside tree that Hippocrates was already prescribing.
extra.verification_notes: Willow bark is the historical source of salicin/salicylic acid that led to aspirin; meadowsweet is a herb, not a tree, so there is no competing answer.

explanation: Willow bark was chewed for fever and aches for thousands of years before salicin was isolated from it in the 1820s and refined into aspirin by Bayer in the 1890s.

question: True or false: green tea and black tea are harvested from two different species of plant.
source_excerpt: Green tea: unwilted and unoxidized. Black tea: wilted, sometimes crushed, and fully oxidized.

extra.why_interesting: The colours and flavours differ so much that many assume separate plants, but the entire difference happens after harvest.
extra.verification_notes: Both green and black tea are made from Camellia sinensis, differing only in processing/oxidation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea).

explanation: Both come from the very same shrub, Camellia sinensis. Black tea leaves are simply allowed to oxidise and darken after picking, while green tea leaves are heated quickly to stop that process.

question: Bamboo can grow taller than a house and is used for scaffolding, yet botanically it is a giant member of which plant family?
source_excerpt: Bamboos are a diverse group of mostly evergreen perennial flowering plants making up the subfamily Bambusoideae of the grass family Poaceae.

extra.why_interesting: Something that forms forests and is used as scaffolding feels like a tree, yet it is a cousin of the lawn.
extra.verification_notes: Bamboo is the subfamily Bambusoideae of the grass family Poaceae, and it is used for scaffolding, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo.

explanation: Bamboo is a woody grass, and it grows like one: some species shoot up nearly a metre in a single day, making them the fastest-growing plants on Earth.

question: The Venus flytrap looks like it belongs in a tropical jungle, but in the wild it grows naturally only in a small patch of coastal wetland in which country?
source_excerpt: native only to the coastal bogs of North and South Carolina in the United States, specifically within a 100-kilometer (62-mile) radius of Wilmington, North Carolina.

extra.why_interesting: Carnivorous plants read as exotic jungle creatures, but this one is a homebody from the American southeast.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Venus flytrap is native only to coastal bogs of North and South Carolina, USA; Florida and Washington populations are introduced.

explanation: Its entire native range lies within about 100 kilometres of Wilmington, North Carolina. Every flytrap anywhere else in the world descends from that one corner of the Carolinas.

question: The tumbleweed rolling through countless Hollywood Westerns is not native to America at all. From which country was it accidentally imported in the 1870s, hidden in a shipment of flaxseed?
source_excerpt: flaxseed from Russia turned out to be contaminated with Salsola seeds

extra.why_interesting: The single most American image in cinema is an immigrant that arrived by accident after the Wild West era had already begun.
extra.verification_notes: Standard accounts say tumbleweed arrived in South Dakota in the 1870s in flaxseed from Russia; a minor Ukraine variant exists, but the region was then in the Russian Empire.

explanation: It is known as Russian thistle, and it arrived in South Dakota around 1873 in contaminated flaxseed. Within two decades it had rolled across most of the western United States.

question: The same hydrangea bush can bloom pink in one garden and blue in another. Which property of the soil decides the colour?
source_excerpt: An acidic soil (pH below 7) will usually produce a flower colour closer to blue, whereas an alkaline soil (pH above 7) will produce flowers of a pink, or even a red colour.

extra.why_interesting: Gardeners assume colour is bred into the plant, but the same bush can change colour if you move it or change what you feed it.
extra.verification_notes: Soil pH (acidity) controls hydrangea colour via aluminium availability: acidic gives blue, alkaline gives pink, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Acidic soil frees up aluminium that the plant absorbs, turning the blooms blue, while alkaline soil keeps them pink. Gardeners add aluminium sulfate or lime to steer the colour.

question: Three of these vegetables are close relatives in the same plant family as deadly nightshade and tobacco. Which one is not?
source_excerpt: The family Solanaceae contains such important food species as the potato (Solanum tuberosum), the tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), the pepper (Capsicum sp) and the aubergine or eggplant (Solanum melongena).

extra.why_interesting: Three everyday vegetables are close cousins of a famous poison plant, and the intuitive outlier (tomato, a 'fruit') is actually a member.
extra.verification_notes: Potato, tomato and aubergine are Solanaceae along with deadly nightshade and tobacco; cucumber is Cucurbitaceae (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solanaceae).

explanation: Potato, tomato and aubergine are all nightshades, which is why Europeans once feared tomatoes were poisonous. The cucumber belongs to the gourd family, alongside melons and pumpkins.

question: In the wild, which common fruit is really an inside-out bundle of hundreds of tiny flowers, pollinated by a wasp that crawls in through a hole at its tip?
source_excerpt: A small opening or ostiole, at the apex of the fruit, is a narrow passage that allows the specialized fig wasp, Blastophaga psenes, to enter and pollinate the flowers.

extra.why_interesting: You never see a fig tree in bloom because the flowers are inside the fruit, and the pollinator has to crawl into it.
extra.verification_notes: Fig is a syconium (inverted cluster of many tiny flowers) pollinated by a fig wasp entering via the ostiole at the apex; no newer development contradicts this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ficus_carica).

explanation: That is why you never see a fig tree flowering: the blossoms bloom hidden inside. Each wild fig species has its own tiny wasp partner, a relationship tens of millions of years old.

question: In 2005 a seed excavated at the ancient fortress of Masada, about 2,000 years old, was planted and sprouted into a tree nicknamed Methuselah. What kind of tree is it?
source_excerpt: In March 2005, one of the ancient date seeds germinated, becoming the oldest seed in the world successfully sprouted. Dr. Sallon named the seedling 'Methuselah'.

extra.why_interesting: A seed older than Christianity, dug out of a ruined desert fortress, simply woke up and grew.
extra.verification_notes: Methuselah is a date palm grown from a ~2,000-year-old Masada seed that germinated in 2005 (seed dug up in the 1960s, planted 2005); no newer event contradicts this.

explanation: It is a Judean date palm, a variety praised by Roman writers that had vanished for centuries. Methuselah turned out to be male, so researchers later sprouted ancient female seeds to produce fruit.

question: The Welwitschia of the Namib Desert can live for well over a thousand years, yet in that whole lifetime it grows how many leaves?
source_excerpt: the oldest being perhaps as much as 2,000 years old

extra.why_interesting: A plant that lives a thousand years should have shed millions of leaves; this one never replaces its first pair.
extra.verification_notes: Welwitschia produces only two permanent leaves that grow throughout its life (cotyledons are temporary seed leaves), and individuals may reach about 2,000 years; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welwitschia

explanation: It keeps the same two leaves for life, growing them continuously from the base while the desert wind shreds the ends into a tangled heap. Charles Darwin called it the platypus of the plant kingdom.

question: Pando in Utah looks like a forest of about 47,000 trees, but it is one organism sharing a single root system across 43 hectares. Which tree is it?
source_excerpt: Pando... quaking aspen (Populus tremuloides)... approximately 47,000 stems... 42.89 hectares

extra.why_interesting: What looks like an ordinary forest is one individual, heavier than a dozen blue whales, and possibly thousands of years old.
extra.verification_notes: Pando is a quaking aspen clone of about 47,000 stems over 42.89 ha, per Wikipedia; no newer developments change this.

explanation: Every trunk of this quaking aspen is a genetically identical shoot from one root network, estimated to weigh around 6,000 tonnes. The colony is thought to be thousands of years old, though it is now struggling against grazing deer.

question: Six trees of one species growing within two kilometres of the Hiroshima bomb's hypocentre survived the blast of 1945 and are still alive today. Which tree, a familiar sight on city streets worldwide, is it?
source_excerpt: Six ginkgo trees located 1–2 km from the Hiroshima bomb site survived the blast

extra.why_interesting: The species is already the sole survivor of a 200-million-year-old lineage, and then it survived an atomic bomb too.
extra.verification_notes: Ginkgo is the species cited for six survivors near the Hiroshima hypocentre; the per-species count could not be fully confirmed on the Hibakujumoku page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibakujumoku).

explanation: The ginkgo is the last survivor of a lineage with fossils over 200 million years old, and its toughness showed again at Hiroshima, where the scorched trees budded the following spring. Seeds from them are now planted around the world as peace trees.

question: Young sunflowers famously swing their heads to follow the sun across the sky, but once the flower head matures it stops moving and settles facing one fixed compass direction for the rest of its life. Which direction?
source_excerpt: Circadian regulation of directional growth pathways accounts for both phenomena and leads to increased vegetative biomass and enhanced pollinator visits to flowers.

extra.why_interesting: Almost everyone 'knows' sunflowers follow the sun, so the player expects the answer to be 'they keep turning' or 'south'. The twist is that the grown-up flower parks itself permanently toward the sunrise, and the reason is a charming piece of bee-marketing.
extra.verification_notes: Atamian et al. 2016 (Science) and follow-up drone studies confirm mature sunflower heads stop moving and face east.

explanation: Facing the sunrise lets the head warm up quickly each morning, and researchers found those warm, east-facing flowers attract far more pollinating bees than ones turned the other way.
